newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swiss file once again tops transport council agenda.
newsitem.headline: Swiss file once again tops transport council agenda.

text.p: Relations between the European Union and Switzerland are once again high on the Transport Council agenda for the two-day meeting beginning on Thursday, EU diplomats said.

Council will hear a European Commission report on how talks with the Swiss are progressing, a point which Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock will hope proceeds more smoothly after his Alpine tour last month of Austria, Italy and France.

The main issues, as ever, relate to road transport and how to set up a coordinated policy on charges, Switzerland's demands for market access and cabotage rights and the EU's reciprocal demand for immediate access for its hauliers' 40-tonne lorries.
Another point of difference remains Switzerland's request for a safeguard clause in the agreement to guard against "crisis situations", for which read any backsliding on an eventual deal.

Ministers will also hear a report on the recent civil aviation talks with the United States, a point on which most member states will already be up to speed given their particpation in the EU delegation which went for initial talks in Washington at the end of October.
Next on the agenda is the Commission's proposal for a Council Directive on the charging of goods vehicles for the use of certain infrastructures, the Eurovignette revision, COM(96)331.
The proposal is intended to replace 93/89/EEC which was annulled by the European Court of Justice on July 5 1995 because of procedural irregularities.

The proposal, applicable to vehicles exceeding 12 tonnes gross weight, suggests retention of the EURO 2 lorry standard and higher charges for EURO 1 and non-EURO vehicles to encourage operators to switch to newer, less-polluting vehicles.

Thursday's discussion will be the Council's second stab at the proposal, with the main issues being how to introduce a differentiated vehicle taxation system with a mandatory user charge, how to incorporate external-costs thinking into toll road charging systems and how to define the criteria governing extra charges related to travel through environmentally sensitive zones.

Other points to discuss include the setting of a maximum tax on vehicles and authorisation for member states to set lower taxes than specified minimum figures when a user charge or toll-road system applies.

Thursday's debate will also tackle the question of external costs, how much the Eurovignette charge should go up and how to relate user charges to infrastructure damage by lorries and to lorries' environmental characteristics.

Ministers' attention will then move to the draft regulation laying down the conditions under which non-resident carriers may operate national road passenger transport services within a member state, a proposal which is intended to revise Regulation 2454/92.

The Commission proposal, COM(95)729, also suggests the liberalisation of cabotage in regular services, a point which has raised a variety of adverse reactions on the question of whether such cabotage is purely internal or international.
October's Council asked the Committee of Permanent Representatives to find a compromise on this including appropriate safeguard clauses, which ministers will discuss on Thursday.
Council is also expected to adopt a common position on proposal COM(96)190 on changing Council Regulation 684/92 on common rules on the international carriage of passengers by coach and bus.
Ministers will hold their second orientation debate on the Commission's White Paper on the future of the railways, COM(96)421, which aims to revive rail's flagging fortunes.

The paper's five main areas of suggested Community action concern ways to improve the sector's financial health, how to build in market forces, maintain public service obligations, integrate national networks and tackle social issues.

Suggestions include extending freight shippers' and passenger carriers' rights of access to national and international rail infrastructure, the creation of freight corridors or freeways and a time-delayed "strict" implementation of Treaty state-aid rules.
An obligation to separate the operation of infrastructure and the provision of rail transport services is also raised as an issue.

Ministers will hold an orientation debate on the Commission's proposal COM(94)323 for a Council regulation amending the Council directive and regulation on recording equipment in road transport (tachographs).

Moving to air transport, ministers will try to tie up the remaining points related to proposal COM(95)724 for a Council regulation on air carrier liabilities in case of accidents, most of which they sorted out in October.

Ministers will also debate the recommendation for a decision to allow the Commission to begin talks for the Community to become a member of Eurocontrol, the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation and the Commission's proposal, adopted on Wednesday, to join the Joint Aviation Authorities.

For Friday's agenda, there is Council's second visit to proposal COM(96)255) for a Council directive setting up a harmonised safety regime for fishing vessels of 24 metres or more in length, which will possibly result in a political accord.

Talks on the proposal for a Council directive amending Council directive 93/75/EEC concerning minimum requirements for vessels bound for or leaving Community ports and carrying dangerous or polluting goods will be only at the level of an orientation debate.
Finally, ministers will discuss, and possibly adopt a resolution on, the Commission's maritime strategy, a central issue is the Commission's planned revision of state aid guidelines.
